# System Intent and Design Lifecycles


When we look at modern computing, our discipline faces a widening capability gap. Hardware and software complexity has grown beyond what traditional manual design loops can effectively explore. Computer architecture has repeatedly expanded what we can build by advancing our design methods alongside our semiconductor devices. In Part I, we address why our discipline must transition to Architecture 2.0, establishing why rising complexity demands AI-native design systems without surrendering human commitment authority.

This transition confronts an immediate tension: the *Verification Crisis*. Generative models and automated search engines can propose thousands of architectural candidates per hour, but physical simulation, formal verification, and expert review remain computationally expensive and strictly bounded. Generating candidate designs provides no engineering value if evaluation capacity cannot keep pace. We introduce the eight-layer Lighthouse prompt stack as our core organizational framework, demonstrating how compact system intent lowers through structured representations into executable hardware under explicit evaluation budgets. A staged design lifecycle and shared ontology then keep that expanding work organized.

::: {.callout-part}
1. How can compact system intent become an executable architecture specification without diluting system obligations or human commitment authority?
2. Why does candidate generation velocity outpace downstream verification capacity, creating critical evaluation bottlenecks across the design loop?
:::
